cards.text: King Solomon is ruling over Israel, and the text starts with his chief officials: priests, secretaries, a recorder, a palace manager, a man over the forced labor and Benaiah son of Jehoiada in charge of the army. That's a LOT of job titles. On my cookie planet I'm every single one of them, and I STILL show up late.

Next come twelve governors over all Israel, region by region, and each one provides food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Two of them are married to Solomon's daughters. I bet those two NEVER miss their month.
Now step back and look at the people of Judah and Israel. They're as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

cards.question: All those people of Judah and Israel are eating and drinking and rejoicing.

cards.text: And Solomon's reign stretches WAY past Israel. He reigns over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, all the way to the border of Egypt.

cards.question: The kingdoms under Solomon rebel against him every chance they get.

cards.text: Then the text lists Solomon's provisions for a single day: thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty range oxen and a hundred sheep, plus deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened poultry. ONE day. I bake every single morning, friend, and I have never once needed a cor of anything.

cards.question: Solomon has dominion over everything west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza. And he has ___ on all sides.
Throughout Solomon's days, Judah and Israel dwell securely from Dan to Beersheba. What picture does the writer use for each man?

answers.text: Under his own vine and fig tree

cards.text: Solomon also has 4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses, and each month the governors take their turn bringing barley and straw for them. Twelve THOUSAND horses, friend, and I can't keep track of ONE timer.

cards.question: The governors see to it that nothing is lacking for King Solomon and all who come to his table.

cards.text: Now here's the part I love. God gives Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight and understanding beyond measure.

cards.question: That picture again! Solomon's understanding is beyond measure, like the ___ on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom is greater than that of all the men of the East, and greater than all the wisdom of ___.

cards.text: He's wiser than all men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and wiser than Heman, Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol. I once got swapped out for a shiny new stamper, so I think I know EXACTLY how Darda feels.

cards.question: Solomon's fame stays inside Israel's borders.
Solomon's songs number a thousand and five, and his proverbs outnumber his songs. How many proverbs does he compose?
Solomon speaks of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall. What else does he teach about?

answers.text: Animals and birds and reptiles and fish
The stars and the moon and the seasons

cards.question: All the kings of the earth hear about Solomon's wisdom. What do they do?

answers.text: Send men to listen to him
Ban his words in their lands

findings.problem: This story card is not the opening card but has three sentences: 'Next come twelve governors…', 'Two of them are married to Solomon's daughters.' and 'I bet those two NEVER miss their month.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: the provisions list, 'ONE day.' and 'I bake every single morning, friend, and I have never once needed a cor of anything.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: 'Like the sand on the seashore' first appears at 1 Kings 4:20, where card 3 tells it. Card 13 asks about it at its second appearance (4:29), and its 'That picture again!' points the baker straight back to card 3's answer.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: The question says the proverbs outnumber the songs, which number a thousand and five. That rules out both wrong answers ('Three hundred' and 'Five hundred'), so the answer is given away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'Under his own vine and fig tree' sounds clearly biblical, while 'Behind his own locked gate' and 'Inside his own stone tower' do not. The right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
